blocks.text: Ten days after a hip replacement, a 68-year-old woman who has been largely bed-bound develops a swollen, tender left calf. Two days later she collapses with sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. A clot that formed quietly in a leg vein has travelled to the lungs.

blocks.markdown: **Haemostasis** is the normal, localised plugging of a vessel defect by platelets and fibrin. **Thrombosis** is the inappropriate formation of a solid mass of blood constituents (platelets, fibrin, red cells and leucocytes) within the vessels or heart of a living person. An **embolus** is a detached intravascular solid, liquid or gaseous mass carried by blood to a site distant from its origin. Most emboli are thromboemboli.

blocks.title: Virchow triad
blocks.text: Thrombosis is promoted by three primary influences: endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence) and hypercoagulability of the blood. Any one may suffice, and they frequently combine.

rows: Exposes subendothelial collagen and tissue factor; loss of antithrombotic properties
Atherosclerotic plaque rupture; myocardial infarction; vasculitis; hypertension; cigarette smoking
Stasis allows platelet contact with endothelium and local accumulation of clotting factors; turbulence damages the endothelium
Atrial fibrillation; aneurysm; immobility; varicose veins
Increased tendency of blood to clot
Factor V Leiden; prothrombin gene variant; pregnancy; oral contraceptive; malignancy; nephrotic syndrome; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

blocks.markdown:
### Morphology of a thrombus

A thrombus that forms in flowing blood has **lines of Zahn**: alternating pale layers of platelets and fibrin and darker layers of red cells. This laminated appearance is evidence that the thrombus formed while blood was flowing, that is, in life. **Arterial thrombi** are usually platelet-rich and begin at sites of endothelial injury or turbulence (for example overlying a ruptured atheromatous plaque). **Venous thrombi** (phlebothrombosis) are usually red or 'stasis' thrombi, rich in red cells, and form in the deep veins of the calf, popliteal and femoral veins.

### Thrombus or post-mortem clot?

After death, blood clots in the vessels. This post-mortem clot differs from a thrombus.

- Post-mortem clot is **gelatinous, soft and rubbery**, with a dark red dependent layer (sedimented red cells) and a yellow 'chicken fat' upper layer (plasma); it is **not attached** to the vessel wall and has **no lines of Zahn**.
- Thrombus is **firm, dry, friable**, with **lines of Zahn**, and is **attached** to the vessel wall at the point of origin.

rows: Dark red and yellow (chicken fat) layers
blocks.caption: Distinguishing features at autopsy.

blocks.title: Which is it at autopsy?
blocks.prompt: At autopsy of a 72-year-old man, a mass lies in the left femoral vein. It is firm, adherent to the wall, with alternating pale and dark layers. A second mass in the right ventricle is soft, gelatinous, glistening and free, with a dark lower layer and a yellow upper layer. Classify both.

steps.text: Femoral mass: adherent, firm and with layering (lines of Zahn) means it formed in flowing blood during life: a thrombus.
Ventricular mass: soft, unattached, with sedimented red cells beneath yellow plasma: a post-mortem clot.
Check with the Virchow triad: the leg thrombus likely reflects stasis (immobility) or hypercoagulability.

blocks.answer: Femoral: ante-mortem thrombus. Ventricular: post-mortem clot.

blocks.markdown:
### Fate of a thrombus

A thrombus may (1) **propagate** along the vessel, (2) be **dissolved** by fibrinolysis (particularly if new), (3) **organise**, being invaded by endothelium and fibroblasts and converted into fibrous tissue, (4) become **recanalised** with new channels, or (5) **embolise**. Infected thrombi may form septic emboli and abscesses.

### Embolism and the path from a deep vein thrombosis

Most pulmonary emboli arise from **deep vein thrombosis (DVT)** of the leg. The embolus travels with venous blood from the leg through the **femoral and external iliac veins**, into the **inferior vena cava**, then the **right atrium**, **right ventricle** and **pulmonary trunk**. It lodges in the pulmonary arteries; a large embolus at the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk is called a **saddle embolus** and may cause sudden death through acute right heart failure. Small emboli lodge in peripheral branches and may cause pulmonary infarcts or be silent. Because the path passes through the right heart into the lungs, venous emboli cause **pulmonary embolism**. In contrast, **systemic (arterial) emboli** originate mostly in the left heart (for example from atrial fibrillation or mural thrombus after myocardial infarction) and lodge in the brain, spleen, kidneys or legs. A venous embolus can cross to the systemic circulation only through an intracardiac defect, a **paradoxical embolus**.

blocks.title: Tracing the path
blocks.prompt: A thrombus forms in the left popliteal vein. List in order the vessels and chambers it passes before lodging in the lung, and name the source of a clot that causes a stroke in a patient with atrial fibrillation.

steps.text: Popliteal vein, then femoral vein, then external iliac vein, then common iliac vein.
Then the inferior vena cava, which empties into the right atrium.
From the right atrium it passes to the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk, and lodges in a pulmonary artery.
In atrial fibrillation the left atrium (especially its appendage) fibrillates, stasis occurs and thrombus forms on the left; embolism goes to the arterial tree and brain, not the lungs.

blocks.answer: Popliteal, femoral, iliac veins, IVC, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary arteries; stroke emboli arise in the left atrium.

items: Other embolic types: fat (after long bone fracture), air (central line, decompression sickness), amniotic fluid and tumour emboli.
Risk factors for DVT include immobility, surgery, malignancy, pregnancy and inherited thrombophilia.
Arterial thrombi are platelet-rich; venous thrombi are fibrin- and red cell-rich.
Anticoagulants prevent propagation and embolisation of existing thrombi (teaching context only).

blocks.title: Direction matters
blocks.text: A venous embolus goes to the lungs; an arterial embolus goes to the systemic organs. Only through a septal defect can a venous clot cause a stroke (paradoxical embolism).

points: Virchow triad comprises endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow and hypercoagulability.
A thrombus is attached, firm and shows lines of Zahn; a post-mortem clot is soft, gelatinous, unattached and lacks lines of Zahn.
A DVT embolus travels through leg veins, the inferior vena cava, right atrium and right ventricle to the pulmonary arteries.

questions.stem: Atrial fibrillation promotes thrombosis in the left atrium mainly through which element of Virchow triad?

distractorRationale.b: Endothelium is not primarily damaged in AF.
distractorRationale.c: Coagulability is not the main change.

questions.explanation: Uncoordinated atrial contraction causes stasis, which allows clotting factors to accumulate and platelets to contact the endothelium. Stasis is one of the three elements of Virchow triad.

questions.stem: A woman who smokes and takes the combined oral contraceptive develops a DVT. Which Virchow triad element is most clearly raised by oestrogen-containing contraceptives?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: oestrogen increases hepatic synthesis of clotting factors.
distractorRationale.c: Stasis is not the main mechanism.

questions.explanation: Oestrogen increases hepatic synthesis of clotting factors, raising coagulability. Smoking adds endothelial injury, so more than one element may combine.

questions.stem: At autopsy, an intravascular mass is gelatinous, glistening, not attached to the vessel wall and shows a yellow upper layer over a dark red lower layer. This is:

options.text: A venous thrombus with lines of Zahn

distractorRationale.b: Arterial thrombi are firm and attached.
distractorRationale.c: Lines of Zahn are absent in post-mortem clot.

questions.explanation: A soft, unattached, gelatinous mass with sedimentation layers (chicken fat) is a post-mortem clot. A thrombus is adherent, firm and shows lines of Zahn.

questions.stem: What microscopic feature proves that a thrombus formed in flowing blood during life?

distractorRationale.b: Granulomas are not part of thrombus.

questions.explanation: Lines of Zahn are alternating layers of platelets/fibrin and red cells deposited as blood flows past. Post-mortem clots do not show them.

questions.stem: A thrombus in the femoral vein breaks off. Which sequence correctly describes its path to a lung?

options.text: Iliac veins, inferior vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery
Iliac arteries, aorta, left ventricle, pulmonary vein
Iliac veins, inferior vena cava, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta
Portal vein, liver, hepatic veins, left atrium

questions.correctOptionText: Iliac veins, inferior vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery

distractorRationale.b: Emboli from veins travel in veins to the right heart.
distractorRationale.c: This would be a paradoxical route through a septal defect, not normal.
distractorRationale.d: The portal vein is not the leg's route.

questions.explanation: Venous return carries the embolus via the inferior vena cava to the right heart and then out through the pulmonary trunk. The lungs are the first capillary-bed filter.

questions.stem: True or false: A thrombus in a leg vein can cause a stroke without any septal defect, because it travels through the aorta to the brain.
questions.explanation: A venous embolus passes to the right heart and lungs, where it is trapped. It can reach the brain only via a patent connection between the right and left sides (paradoxical embolism).

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a recent anterior myocardial infarction develops sudden weakness of the right arm and leg. Which source is the most likely?

options.text: Mural thrombus on the damaged left ventricular wall
Deep vein thrombus in the calf
Fat emboli from a long bone

questions.correctOptionText: Mural thrombus on the damaged left ventricular wall

distractorRationale.a: Correct: endothelial injury and stasis over the infarct generate a mural thrombus.
distractorRationale.b: Calf thrombus would cause pulmonary embolism.

questions.explanation: Infarcted myocardium injures the endocardium and impairs wall motion, so thrombus forms on the left ventricle. Fragments enter the systemic circulation and can lodge in the brain.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man dies suddenly three days after a knee arthroscopy. Autopsy shows a large embolus astride the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk. What is the most likely mechanism of death?

options.text: Acute right heart failure from obstruction of pulmonary outflow
Air embolism of the coronary arteries

questions.correctOptionText: Acute right heart failure from obstruction of pulmonary outflow

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a saddle embolus blocks both pulmonary arteries.
distractorRationale.b: Paradoxical embolism needs a septal defect and nothing suggests it.
distractorRationale.c: Rupture is a complication of infarction.
distractorRationale.d: No source of air is described.

questions.explanation: A saddle embolus obstructs both main pulmonary arteries, so the right ventricle cannot eject and cardiac output collapses. This is the typical cause of sudden death from massive pulmonary embolism.

questions.stem: State the three components of Virchow triad and give one clinical example of each.
markingGuide: Endothelial injury, e.g. atheromatous plaque rupture or myocardial infarction
Abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence), e.g. atrial fibrillation, immobility, aneurysm
Hypercoagulability, e.g. factor V Leiden, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, malignancy
questions.explanation: Thrombus formation is promoted by wall injury, flow disturbance and blood changes. Each has several clinical examples.

questions.stem: At autopsy you find a mass in a pulmonary artery. Describe how you would distinguish a thrombus from a post-mortem clot and why it matters.
markingGuide: Thrombus firm, dry, friable, adherent to wall
Post-mortem clot soft, gelatinous, not attached, with red and chicken-fat layers
Matters because a thrombus or embolus indicates a cause of death or pathology in life, whereas post-mortem clot is a postmortem artefact
questions.explanation: Attachment, consistency and lines of Zahn separate a life-time thrombus from a post-mortem change. This distinction determines whether the finding contributed to death.
